RagShortTexts: Royal Forest Laws claimed vert and venison exclusively for the King, punishable by blinding.

Variants.Content: The Norman kings marked off large parts of England as royal forest, land set aside for the king's own hunting. Forest law kept two things apart: vert, the timber and undergrowth that shaded the deer, and venison, the game animals themselves. Clearing trees or keeping dogs that had not been maimed was an offence, since a dog could chase the deer out of the forest. A man caught taking a royal stag could lose his eyes or a limb, and the severity of these penalties gave the greenwood a long tradition of outlaw songs and legends.

The Charter of the Forest of 1217 reined in the worst royal excesses by replacing capital punishment with heavy fines. Verderers and forest wardens still pressed arbitrary dues on freemen of the shires, so the charter did not end the burden. A lord who held land along a forest edge had to judge which officials could be trusted and which would extract money at every turn.
In royal oak forests, poachers grease bowstrings to loose shafts into the dusk. Salting illicit venison inside hay ricks feeds starving families when winter blizzards ruin harvest stores.
